reading.body:
AI's physical supply chain is now treated as a distinct insurance class, with cover spanning GPU cargo, Taiwan foundry concentration, cooling failures, and multi-year grid equipment delays.

The ten cover types map to the full physical path of an AI cluster: fabrication in Taiwan, transit of high-value accelerators, installation and cooling, grid connection, and civil works. Each point is a place where a single failure can idle compute that has already been paid for.

The inclusion of transformer and switchgear lead times of two to four years, and delay in startup on fibre trenching, ties insurance directly to the power and buildings bottleneck. Coverage exists because these delays are now expected parts of AI deployment, not rare exceptions.

What the list does not show is cost, capacity, or loss history. It records that insurers have named these risks, not how much protection is actually being bought or at what price.

The ten cover types are not ten independent risks. They are ten points on one serial path, and the path has no redundancy. Fabrication in Taiwan feeds transit, transit feeds installation, installation feeds cooling, cooling feeds the grid connection, and the grid connection feeds civil works. A failure at any single point idles compute that has already been paid for, which is why the list reads as a sequence rather than a menu.

Two of the ten sit upstream of the cluster itself. Foundry concentration risk and rare earth export bottlenecks are the only points that describe a constraint on making the hardware rather than on moving, housing, or powering it. The other eight all assume the accelerators exist and are trying to reach a building with power.

The lead times are the tell. Transformer and switchgear at two to four years, and fibre trenching delay, are the only items on the list measured in years rather than in incidents. That is a different kind of risk from a pump failure or a pallet dropped in transit. A pump can be replaced inside a maintenance window. A transformer cannot, so the schedule risk and the equipment risk are being covered by the same class of policy even though they behave nothing alike.

What does a single pallet of GPUs actually carry in insured value?
The data says a single pallet carries millions in accelerators but gives no figure beyond that. It does not hold a per-pallet value, a shipment count, or a total sum insured.

Why is Taiwan named specifically rather than semiconductor supply generally?
Because leading edge fabrication is concentrated there, and the cover is written as contingent business interruption against that geographic concentration. The data does not say what share of leading edge capacity sits on the island.

How long can a grid equipment delay run?
Two to four years for transformers and switchgear. That is the longest horizon anywhere on the list and the only item that can outlast a typical construction schedule.

Are refurbished accelerators insurable?
Yes, through third party products covering performance degradation in refurbished hardware. The data does not say what degradation threshold triggers a claim or how refurbished units are priced against new ones.

What can destroy a running cluster without any supply chain event at all?
Three things on the list: thermal shock when cooling is lost suddenly, high pressure pump failures in direct to chip systems, and airborne particulates contaminating an advanced packaging facility. The first two are on site, the third is upstream at packaging.

Does the data show what any of this cover costs or how much is bought?
No. It records that insurers have named these ten risks, not the premiums, the limits, or the loss history behind them.
